result: Visual landmarks control the orientation of MEC spatial representations. The firing fields of grid cells, border cells, and irregular spatially selective neurons rotated to follow the position of LED light panels, with peak correlations at 90° and 180° matching the angular separation between lights.
evaluation: Claims C18-C20 provide converging evidence that light panels acted as dominant polarization cues. The rotation of firing fields (C18) and quantitative correlation analysis (C19) directly support this conclusion, which is appropriately inferred in C20.

result: Grid cell periodicity rapidly degrades in darkness but is initially preserved. Grid scores and information scores were significantly lower during dark trials compared to light trials. The stable periodic pattern was only present during the first 30 seconds in darkness, and reinstatement of the grid pattern by visual stimuli occurred over several seconds.
evaluation: Claims C21-C29 form a coherent narrative supported by statistical analysis (C22, C23, C26) and temporal dynamics (C25-C29). The findings are replicated across individual mice (C23) and supported by appropriate statistical tests. The inference that visual landmarks are required (C24) is well-justified by the data.

result: Firing rate associations between grid cells are largely preserved in darkness despite spatial instability. Correlations of firing rate associations remained high (r=0.926) during dark trials, though median firing rates were slightly lower.
evaluation: Claims C30-C32 demonstrate preserved firing associations with strong statistical support (r=0.968 for light-light, r=0.926 for light-dark). The slight reduction in firing rate (C33) is statistically significant but modest. This dissociation between spatial and rate coding is well-documented.

result: Distance coding by grid cells is partially preserved in darkness but impaired. Spike-triggered maps showed reduced grid scores in darkness, and distance scores were lower but still above chance levels. The ring of activity in some spike-triggered maps suggests unstable grid orientation.
evaluation: Claims C34-C39 provide multiple lines of evidence for partial preservation of distance coding. Statistical tests show significant impairment (C34, C36) but above-chance performance (C37). The inference about translational drift (C35) and orientation instability (C39) are appropriately cautious and supported by the data patterns.

result: Speed coding in MEC neurons is modulated by visual information. 34.55% of MEC neurons showed significant speed modulation. Most speed-modulated cells had lower firing rates at given speeds during dark trials, with steeper slopes and higher intercepts during light trials. The median firing rate change from dark to light was 12.36%.
evaluation: Claims C40-C50 provide comprehensive characterization of speed coding changes with visual input. Statistical analyses are appropriate and consistent across multiple measures (slopes, intercepts, speed scores). The sample size (n=304 speed cells from 880 neurons) is adequate. The conclusion that speed coding depends on both self-motion and visual cues (C50) is well-supported.

result: Parvalbumin-expressing interneurons are enriched for speed-modulated cells and receive local excitatory input that is reduced in darkness. 51.4% of PV neurons were speed-modulated versus 27.1% of other neurons. Analysis of functional connections showed that presynaptic neurons to speed cells had reduced firing in darkness.
evaluation: Claims C51-C57 provide mechanistic insight into speed coding changes. The enrichment of speed cells in PV population (C51) is statistically significant. The functional connectivity analysis (C52-C56) uses appropriate methods (crosscorrelation) though the number of identified connections is small (61/10,880). The mechanistic inference (C57) is appropriately cautious ('some' interneurons, 'can be explained').

result: Border cell firing becomes less confined to environmental boundaries in darkness. Both the concentration of firing at the periphery (DM) and map polarity were significantly reduced during dark trials.
evaluation: Claims C58-C59 are supported by statistical analysis (n=63 border cells, p<10^-7 and p<10^-6). However, when using mouse-level statistics, the polarity reduction did not reach significance (p=0.11), suggesting some variability across animals. The result is supported but with noted limitations.

result: Head-direction selectivity is reduced in darkness. Head-direction vector length was significantly lower during dark trials compared to light trials for 85 recorded head-direction cells.
evaluation: Claims C60-C61 are straightforward and well-supported by statistical analysis (p<10^-15). The effect is consistent when analyzed at the mouse level (p=0.0078) and when restricted to MEC tetrodes (p<10^-10).

result: A majority of MEC neurons (57.2%) change their firing rate between light and dark conditions, with most neurons (76.74%) reducing their firing rate in darkness. Border cells were more likely than grid cells to show rate changes, but interneurons and principal cells showed similar probabilities of rate changes.
evaluation: Claims C62-C66 provide comprehensive population-level analysis with appropriate statistics. The median rate discrimination index (0.072) is significantly positive (p<10^-16). The differential sensitivity of border cells (C65) is statistically significant (p=0.037), though the effect is modest. The lack of difference between interneurons and principal cells (C66) is appropriately reported as non-significant.

result: In a 1D linear track environment, approximately half of MEC neurons showed firing rate changes between two visual contexts (l1 and l2) that differed only in LED patterns, while spatial information and field locations remained largely stable. 70.8% of neurons showed rate changes between light and dark conditions.
evaluation: Claims C67-C79 describe a well-controlled experiment demonstrating context-specific rate coding. The high correlation between l1 and l2 maps (r=0.92, C72) indicates stable field locations, while significant proportions of neurons show rate changes (C75, C78). The inference that firing rate conveys contextual information (C79) is well-supported. However, the proportion of neurons showing changes in MEC-only recordings (35.3%, C77) is notably lower than for all recordings (51.1%, C75), suggesting some contribution from parasubiculum.

result: Grid cell instability in darkness is greater than previously reported, with instability detectable within the first few seconds. The authors propose that the lack of walls in the circular arena, repeated reorientations, and altered border cell representations may have contributed to this rapid error accumulation.
evaluation: Claims C80-C82 are supported by the experimental data. The comparison to previous studies (C81) is appropriate. However, claims C83-C84 are largely speculative explanations for the observed instability. C83 is a methodological description, while C84 explicitly includes speculation ('might have contributed'). The overall conclusion (C85) is appropriately cautious ('faster than previously thought').

result: The speed code in MEC is not context-invariant as previously thought, but shows important contributions from visual cues. Speed-modulated neurons include both high-firing-rate interneurons (enriched in PV-expressing cells) and spatially selective neurons. Speed-modulated neurons are found in multiple brain regions.
evaluation: Claims C86-C87 accurately represent prior work (Kropff et al., 2015). Claim C88 appropriately challenges this view with the current findings, though it includes speculation about optic flow. Claims C89-C90 are well-supported by the data. Claim C91 is a general statement supported by multiple citations. The overall result appropriately contextualizes the findings within existing literature.

result: MEC network activity varies with visual cues, with border cells showing particular sensitivity. The authors speculate that the postrhinal cortex projection, which carries visual information and has depolarizing effects on MEC neurons, may be more active when visual landmarks are present.
evaluation: Claims C92-C94 are well-supported by the experimental data. However, claims C95-C97 are largely speculative. While C95-C96 cite anatomical studies, C97 is explicitly speculative ('tempting to speculate') and lacks direct experimental support. The proposed mechanism is plausible but untested, making the overall result uncertain regarding the mechanistic explanation.

result: Grid cell rate coding in 1D environments is context-specific, with approximately half of grid cells changing firing rates based on nonmetric contextual cues. This occurs independently of behavioral demands, as mice did not need to change behavior following contextual changes.
evaluation: Claims C98-C99 are directly supported by the linear track experiment. Claims C100-C102 appropriately contextualize the findings relative to prior work (Keene et al., 2016) and clarify the experimental design. Claim C103 is speculative ('might take place') but appropriately cautious. The overall result is well-supported.

result: Rate changes within stable firing fields in MEC neurons are consistent with similar phenomena observed in hippocampal place cells. The high correlations between linear firing rate maps suggest minimal changes in field location. The firing rate of grid cells in 1D paths provides information about both position and visual cues.
evaluation: Claims C104-C106 appropriately cite relevant literature showing similar phenomena in hippocampus. Claim C107 provides data-driven inference about field stability. Claim C108 is a broader inference about functional significance that is supported by the data but includes some speculation about real-world navigation. Overall well-supported.

result: The study's main findings reveal that removal of visual landmarks causes profound impairment in grid cell periodicity, changes in speed coding, reduced confinement of border cell activity, widespread firing rate changes in MEC neurons, and context-specific rate coding in response to nonmetric visual cues.
evaluation: Claims C109-C114 summarize the main findings of the study. All are directly supported by the experimental data presented. C114 appropriately synthesizes the findings into a broader conclusion about context specificity in MEC rate coding. This represents a well-supported summary of the major results.

result: Histological verification confirmed that most recording sites (75.51%) were in the MEC, with 86.49% of MEC tetrode tracks reaching layer II. A total of 880 neurons were recorded across 8 mice in 89 sessions.
evaluation: Claims C15-C17 provide essential methodological information about recording locations and sample sizes. These are straightforward descriptive claims supported by histological data and experimental records.

result: The introduction reviews established knowledge about grid cells, including their periodic firing patterns, reliance on self-motion cues, integration of heading direction and distance, dependence on head-direction and speed cell inputs, error accumulation without external corrections, and the influence of visual landmarks on grid patterns.
evaluation: Claims C1-C14 are all citation-based claims from the introduction that accurately represent prior work. These provide appropriate context for the current study and are well-supported by the cited literature.
